A HOMILY ON REPENTANCE, delivered when he had returned from the countryside. [279] Homily 1.

1. Did you remember us during this time we were apart from you? I, for my part, was never able to forget you. Though I left the city, I did not leave behind my memory of you. Those who love beautiful bodies carry the sight they long for with them wherever they go. In the same way we, having fallen in love with the beauty of your soul, always carry the loveliness of your mind about with us. Painters mix various colours to produce likenesses of bodies. So we too took your zeal at the assemblies, your eagerness to listen, your goodwill toward the speaker and all your other good deeds, and mixed them like the various colours of virtue. We sketched the character of your soul, set it before the eyes of our mind, and through this picture found consolation enough for our absence. We turned these things over continually, sitting at home and rising up, walking and resting, coming in and going out, dreaming of your love. Not only by day but at night too we revelled in these imaginings. What Solomon said, "I sleep, but my heart is awake," we too experienced then. The need for sleep weighed down our eyelids, but the tyranny of our love for you kept the eyes of our mind awake, and often I seemed to be talking with you in a dream. For the soul naturally pictures at night whatever it has been thinking about by day, and that is what happened to us then. Though I did not see you with the eyes of the flesh, I saw you with the eyes of love. Though I was not present with you in body, I was present with you in affection, and my ears rang constantly with your acclamation. That is why, when bodily illness obliged me to stay there longer and to enjoy the benefit of the air for the health of my flesh, the force of your love would not put up with it. It cried out, and it did not stop troubling me until it had persuaded me to get up even before the proper time, and had counselled me to count your company as health and delight and every good thing whatever. Persuaded by it, we chose to come back while still carrying the remnants of the illness, rather than shake off the body's weakness entirely and grieve your love any longer. For while I was staying there I heard your complaints, and a stream of letters brought them to me, and I paid attention to those who were complaining no less than to those who [?] …

[Apparatus: Colbert manuscript: "Of our father among the saints … Chrysostom, on his coming from the countryside after some time, and on repentance." Colbert: "to us."]

… for in natural births this is impossible. [281] Why did he not say, "My little children, whom I am begetting again," but "with whom I am in labour"? Yet elsewhere he does say that he begot them: "For in Christ Jesus I begot you." There he wanted only to show the kinship. Here he was eager to show the pain as well. And how can he call them children when they have not yet been born? If he is in labour, he has not yet given birth, so how can he call them children? So that you may learn that these are not the first birth pangs he is suffering for them. That was enough to shame them. "I became your father once," he says, "and I endured the labour I owed for you, and you also became children once. How then can you throw me into a second labour? The pains of the first births were enough. Why do you stretch me on the rack of these pangs again?" For the falls of the faithful gave him no less pain than those who had not yet believed. It was unbearable to see people who had shared in such great mysteries deserting to impiety. So he cried out very bitterly, with more feeling than any woman, saying, "My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you." He said this because he wanted both to encourage and to frighten them at once. Showing that Christ had not been formed in them struck them with anguish and fear. Making clear that he could be formed gave them courage again. The words "until he is formed" point to both: that he has not yet been formed, and that he can still be formed. If that were not possible, it would have been pointless for him to say to them, "until Christ is formed in you," and he would have been feeding them on empty hopes.

2. Knowing this, let us not despair, but let us not simply grow careless either, for both are ruinous. Despair does not let the fallen get up, and carelessness makes the one who stands fall. Carelessness usually robs us of the goods we have gained, and despair does not let us escape the evils that weigh on us. Contempt brings people down even from heaven itself, and despair leads them down into the very abyss of wickedness, just as refusing to despair makes one run quickly back up even from there. Consider the power of each. The devil was good before this, but through carelessness and despair he fell into such wickedness that he could never rise again. To see that he was good, hear what is said: "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven." The comparison with lightning shows both the brightness of his former life and the swiftness of his fall. Paul was a blasphemer, a persecutor and a man of violence, but because he was zealous and did not despair, he rose and became equal to the angels. Judas was an apostle, but through carelessness he became a traitor. Again, the thief, after all his wickedness, did not despair, and so he entered paradise before anyone else. The Pharisee was overconfident and was brought down from the very height of virtue. The tax collector did not despair, and he was raised up so far that he outran the Pharisee. Do you want me to show you a whole city that did this too? The city of Nineveh was saved in its entirety this way. And yet the sentence had driven them to despair, for he did not say, [282] "If they repent, they will be saved," but simply …

[Apparatus: Savile: "and the one standing." Some manuscripts: ἐκοίνωσε; others: ἐκοινώνησε.]

[?] … the one who did this deed [?] …; he said, "so that we may not be outwitted by Satan," for it is an outwitting [?]. "Were you not rather zealous [?]"? No, but what? "Ought you not rather to have mourned," as though a common disease and plague had seized the city? He is all but saying, "There is need of prayer, confession and supplication, so that the disease may be driven out of the whole city." Do you see how much fear he hung over them? Because they thought the danger stopped with that one man, he fills them with anxiety by saying, "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" What he means is this: "The evil is on the move, and it will reach the other members too. So you must think like people deliberating about an evil that is common to all." Do not tell me that he alone sinned. Consider rather that the danger is a kind of gangrene, and it spreads over the whole rest of the body. When a house is on fire, even those the disaster has not yet reached hurry no less than those caught in it, and contribute everything they have, so that the fire does not press on and come to their own doors. In the same way Paul rouses these people too, saying: "It is a fire. Let us get ahead of the danger. Let us put out the blaze before it seizes the Church." If you make light of the sin because it happened in someone else's body, you are wrong even so, for that man is a member of the whole body.

3. But consider this as well: if you are careless and overlook it, it will seize you too some day. So if not for your brother's sake, then at least for your own, rouse yourself. Check the plague, stop the gangrene before it takes hold, and cut off its spread. Having said this and more, and having ordered that the man be handed over to Satan, Paul says later, once he had changed and become better: "For such a one this punishment by the majority is enough. So confirm your love for him." He had made him a common enemy and foe to all, driven him out of the flock and cut him off from the body. Now see how much zeal he shows in fastening him back and joining him to it again. He did not simply say, "Love him," but "confirm your love for him," that is, show him a firm and unshaken friendship. Bring in a goodwill that is warm, fervent and on fire, matching your former hostility. What has happened, tell me? Did you not hand him over to Satan? "Yes," he says, "but not so that he would stay in Satan's hands. It was so that he would quickly be freed from his tyranny." But, as I was saying, see how Paul fears despair as a great weapon of the devil. Having said, "Confirm your love for him," he adds the reason: "so that such a one may not be swallowed up by excessive sorrow." "The sheep is in the wolf's throat," he says. "Let us hurry, then, and snatch it away first, before he swallows our member and destroys it. The ship is now in a storm. Let us make haste to save it before it is wrecked." When the sea rises and the waves crest on every side, the vessel goes under. In the same way, when despondency closes in on a soul from every side, it quickly drowns unless it has someone to stretch out a hand. Sorrow over sins is saving, but in excess it becomes ruinous. And see how precisely he spoke. He did not say, "so that the devil may not destroy him," but what? "So that … not …"

[Apparatus, partly illegible: [?] … earlier editions had προαρπάσωμεν … "by us" and [?] forgives all sins [?]. Colbert: "changed"; then "that which comes from poverty."]

[?] … baptism one cannot receive the patrimony or accept an inheritance. Through all these details, then, he hints to us at the order of the faithful. Moreover, he was the brother of the son who had done well, and no one could be a brother without spiritual rebirth. So this man fell into the depths of wickedness, and what does he say? "I will go back to my father." This was why the father let him go and did not stop him from going off to a foreign land: so that he might learn well, by experience, how much kindness he had enjoyed while he stayed at home. Often, when God's words do not persuade, he leaves the teaching to the experience of events. This is what he said to the Jews as well. He had spent countless words on them through the prophets without persuading them or drawing them to himself. So he let them be disciplined by punishment, and he says to them, "Your apostasy will discipline you, and your wickedness will reprove you." He ought to have been believed even before events turned out as he said. But they were so unfeeling that they distrusted his exhortations and counsels, so to check their wickedness in advance [?], he lets them be taught by events, in order to win them back that way. So when the prodigal had gone off to the foreign land, learned through hard experience how great an evil it is to fall from a father's house, and come back, the father bore no grudge but received him with open arms. Why? Because he was a father, not a judge. And then there were dances, feasts and celebrations, and the whole house was bright and full of joy. What are you saying? Are these the rewards of wickedness? Not of wickedness, my friend, but of coming back. Not of sin, but of repentance. Not of evil, but of change for the better. And what is more, the elder son was indignant at all this, but the father gently won him over too, saying, "You were always with me, but this one was lost and has been found; he was dead and has come back to life." "When the lost have to be saved," he says, "it is no time for law courts or strict inquiry, but only for kindness and pardon." No doctor neglects to apply medicine to a sick man and demands instead that he give an account of his disorderly life and pay a penalty. And if he had to pay a penalty at all, he paid penalty enough in his stay in the foreign land [?]. For so long a time he was cut off from our company, and he lived on in affliction and disgrace, wrestling with the worst of evils. That is why he says, "He was lost and has been found; he was dead and has come back to life." "Do not look at the present," he says, "but consider how great his former disaster was. You are looking at a brother, not a stranger." He came back to a father who is unable to remember anything of the past, or rather …

[Apparatus: Savile: πατριέιαν [?].]

… for ever and ever. Amen.

And on the dejection of King Ahab, and on Jonah the prophet.
1. Last Sunday you saw a war and a victory: the devil's war and Christ's victory. You saw how repentance was praised, and how the devil could not bear the blow, but was afraid and trembled.

… repentance seized his goods, tore down his very citadel, and dealt him a mortal wound. You will know this, beloved, from what experience showed the other day. Why, then, do we not enjoy such a homily every time, and come to church every day to embrace repentance? Even if you are a sinner, come into the church, so that you may confess your sins. And if you are righteous, come in, so that you may not fall away from righteousness. For the [?] is a harbour for both.

Are you a sinner? Do not despair, but come in, holding up repentance before you. Have you sinned? Say to God, "I have sinned." What toil is there in this? What long road? What affliction, what hardship is there in saying one word, "I have sinned"? Even if you do not call yourself a sinner, do you not have the devil as your accuser? Get in ahead of him and snatch his office away from him, for accusing is his office. Why, then, do you not get ahead of him, confess your sin and wipe out the offence, knowing that your accuser is one who cannot keep quiet? Have you sinned? Come into the church and say to God, "I have sinned." I ask nothing else of you but this alone. For the divine Scripture says, "Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified." Confess the sin, so that you may undo the sin. There is no toil in this, no long speech, no expense of money, nothing else of the kind. Say one word, be honest about your sin, and say, "I have sinned." "And how do we know," someone asks, "that if I confess my sin first, I undo the sin?" In Scripture I have both the one who confessed and was released, and the one who did not confess and was condemned. Cain killed his brother Abel. He was gripped by envy, so that murder followed upon envy, for he took him out into the field and slew him. And what does God say to him? "Where is Abel your brother?" He who knows all things asks, not because he does not know, but to draw the murderer to repentance. That he did not ask out of ignorance he showed by asking, "Where is Abel your brother?" [288] And Cain said, "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" Very well, you are not his keeper. Why were you his slayer, then? You did not guard him; why did you also kill him? Still, you admit these things [?]: you are answerable for guarding him too. What, then, does God say to him? "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth." He convicted him at once and brought punishment on him, not so much for the murder as for the shamelessness. For God does not hate the sinner so much as the one who is shameless about it. That is why he does not accept Cain when he comes to repentance: he did not confess his sin first. For what does he say? "My sin is too great for me to be forgiven," meaning, "I have sinned greatly; I am not worthy to live." What, then, does God say to him? "You shall be groaning and trembling on the earth." And he pronounced a terrible and harsh punishment on him. "I do not kill you," he says, "so that the truth may not be handed over to oblivion …"

[Apparatus: [?] … (one manuscript reads) λόγον εἰπόν, where others and the printed editions have λόγον εἰπών. Some manuscripts: "the one who has sinned."]

… says, "Lawless, most accursed man, adulterer and murderer, you received such honours from God, and you trampled on his commandments?" Nathan said nothing of the kind, so as not to make him more shameless still, for sins exposed in public provoke the sinner to shamelessness. So he comes to him and weaves the drama of a lawsuit. And what does he say? "O king, I have a case to bring before you. There was a rich man and there was a poor man. The rich man had herds and many flocks. The poor man had one ewe lamb, which drank from his cup, ate from his table and slept in his bosom." Here he shows the man's true affection for his wife. "A stranger came, and the rich man spared his own animals, took the poor man's lamb and slaughtered it." Do you see how he weaves the drama here, keeping the blade hidden in the sponge? What, then, does the king do? Thinking that he was passing judgment on someone else, he handed down the harshest sentence. For that is what people are like: against others they are glad to pass sentences, and pass them severely. And what does David say? "As the Lord lives, such a man deserves death, and he shall repay the lamb fourfold." What, then, does Nathan do? He did not soften the blow over many hours. He reveals it at once and makes the sharpest cut, so as not to steal away the feeling of the pain: "You are the man, O king." What, then, does the king say? "I have sinned against the Lord." He did not say, "Who are you to reprove me? Who sent you to speak so boldly? How dare you do this?" He said nothing of the kind, but acknowledged the sin. And what does he say? "I have sinned against the Lord." What, then, does Nathan say to him? "And the Lord has put away your sin. You condemned yourself; I remit the condemnation for you. You confessed honestly; you have undone the sin. You brought the condemnation on yourself; [290] I have undone the sentence." Do you see how the Scripture was fulfilled that says, "Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified"? What toil is there in confessing your sin first?

3. You have another road of repentance too. What is it? Mourning for your sin. Have you sinned? Mourn, and you undo the sin. What toil is there in this? I ask nothing more of you than that you mourn for your sin. I do not tell you to cross seas or put in at harbours, to make a journey or set off on an endless road, to pay out money or make your way through wild waves. What, then? Mourn over your sin. "And how do we know," someone asks, "that if I mourn, I undo the sin?" You have proof of this too from the divine Scripture. There was a king called Ahab. He is spoken of as righteous [?], but he reigned for evil under the influence of Jezebel his wife. He coveted the vineyard of a certain Naboth the Jezreelite, and sent to him saying, "Give me your vineyard, which I have set my heart on, and either take silver from me or another place in exchange." And Naboth said, "God forbid that I should …"

[Apparatus: Manuscripts: "of the murder" (for "of the pain"). Some manuscripts: "the cause."]

… "The earth is the Lord's, and all that fills it." To the sea, then? Do you not know that "the sea is his, and he made it"? To heaven, then? Have you not heard David say, "I will look at the heavens, the work of your fingers"? All the same, Jonah, gripped by fear, fled, or so it seemed, for it is impossible truly to flee from God. Yet when the sea gave him back and he came to Nineveh, he preached, saying, "Three more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown." He gave himself up to flight because he had this in mind: that God, being loving, relents over the evil he has threatened against them, and Jonah himself would then look like a false prophet. And he shows this himself, so that you may learn it [?]. After preaching in Nineveh he went out of the city and watched to see what would happen. When he saw the three days pass and none of the threatened things happen anywhere, he brings up his original reasoning again and says, "Are these not the words I spoke, that God is merciful and patient and relents over the evils of men?" So that Elijah would not suffer anything like what Jonah suffered, God tells him why he pardoned Ahab. And what does God say to Elijah? "Have you seen how Ahab went about mourning and downcast before me? I will not act according to his wickedness." How wonderful! The master becomes the advocate of the slave, and God makes a defence to one man on behalf of another. "Do not think," he says, "that I simply pardoned him. He reformed his ways, and I changed my anger and set it aside. And this is so that you may not be taken for a false prophet. You spoke the truth: had he not changed his ways, he would have had to suffer the sentence. But he did change his ways, and I set my anger aside." And [292] God says to Elijah, "Have you seen how Ahab went about mourning and downcast? I will not act according to my anger." Do you see that mourning wipes out sins?

4. You also have a third road of repentance. I have spoken of many roads of repentance so that, by offering a variety of roads, I may make salvation easy for you. What is this third road? Humility. Be humble, and you have loosed the chains of your sins. You have proof of this too from the divine Scripture, from the reading about the tax collector and the Pharisee. "The Pharisee and the tax collector," it says, "went up to the temple to pray, and the Pharisee began to count up his virtues: 'I am not a sinner like all the world, nor like this tax collector.'" Wretched and miserable soul! You condemned the whole world; why did you also have to wound your neighbour? Was the world not enough for you, unless you condemned the tax collector too? By this you slandered everyone, and did not spare even that one man. "I am not like all the world, nor like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of my possessions to the poor." He uttered words of boasting. Wretched man …

[Apparatus: Some manuscripts: "he shows himself." One manuscript: "wretched and insatiable in soul." Two others: "wretched and [?] in soul."]

…clothed with, the pillar of the Churches, the earthly angel, the heavenly man. I gladly linger over this man, gazing at the beauty of his virtue. The rising sun, sending out its bright rays, does not delight my eyes as much as the face of Paul lights up my mind. The sun gives light to the eyes, but Paul gives them wings up to the very vaults of heaven. He makes the soul loftier than the sun and higher than the moon. Such is the power of virtue: it makes a human being an angel and gives the soul wings to rise to heaven. Paul teaches us this virtue; let us strive to become imitators of his virtue. But we must not wander from our subject. To show… [Savile: "having stripped bare."] BY THE SAME AUTHOR, A DISCOURSE On almsgiving, and on the ten virgins.

1. Do you know where our discourse began last time, or where it ended, or from what subject the words of the previous homily started and to what subject they came? I think you have forgotten where our discourse stopped. I know, but I do not blame you for it or accuse you. Each of you has a wife, looks after children, and cares for everything in the household. Some of you are busy with military service, others are craftsmen, and each of you is occupied with different needs. We, however, spend our time on these things, study these things, and pass our days in them. So you are not to be blamed for this; you are rather to be praised for your zeal, because you do not leave us a single Sunday, but disregard everything and come to church. This is the greatest glory of our city: not its bustle and its suburbs, nor its houses with gilded ceilings and their dining halls, but its having a people that is earnest and wide awake. We recognize the nobility of a tree not from its leaves but from its fruit. This is why we are honored above the irrational animals: because we have reason, share in the word, and love the word. A human being who does not love the word is far more irrational than the beasts, since he does not know why he was honored or where his honor comes from. The prophet put it well: "Man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them." You are a rational being, and you do not love the word? Tell me, what excuse will you have? So you who are lifted on wings toward the word of virtue, and who put everything second to the divine words, are dearer to me than all. Come then, let us take up our subject and what was said previously… [?] the discourse on almsgiving [?]. [Variants: "where it ended"; "or where it ended"; "whence we began, or where we stopped, or from what subject"; "or where we stopped in the previous homily"; "and he cares for all the affairs of the house"; shortly after, "others among craftsmen, and each of you is occupied" [?].] …mourning and downcast: "I will not act according to my

anger." Then we also taught a third road of repentance, and brought forward from Scripture the Pharisee and the tax collector: the Pharisee, boasting arrogantly, lost his righteousness, while the tax collector, by humbling himself, went down rich in the fruit of righteousness. Without spending a single labor he became righteous; he gave words and received deeds. Come then, let us follow the sequence and set out a fourth road of repentance. Which is it? I mean almsgiving, the queen of the virtues, which swiftly lifts people up to the vaults of heaven, the best of advocates. Almsgiving is a great thing. That is why Solomon cried out, "A man is a great thing, and a merciful man is precious." Great are the wings of almsgiving: it cuts through the air, passes the moon, rises beyond the rays of the sun, and climbs to the very vaults of heaven. Yet it does not stop even there: it passes through heaven itself, runs past the multitudes of angels, the choirs of archangels, and all the higher powers, and stands beside the royal throne itself. Learn this from Scripture itself, which says: "Cornelius, your prayers and your alms have gone up before God." And "before God" means this: even if you have many sins, if almsgiving is your advocate, do not be afraid. None of the powers above stands against it. It demands payment of a debt, carrying in its hands its own written bond. For it is the voice of the Master himself: "Whoever does it to one of the least of these has done it to me." So however many other sins you have, your almsgiving outweighs them all.

2. Or do you not know the example of the ten virgins in the Gospel, how those who had no almsgiving, though they had practiced virginity, remained outside the bridal chamber? "There were," it says, "ten virgins, five foolish and five wise. The wise had oil, but the foolish had no oil, and their lamps were going out. The foolish came to the wise and said, 'Give us oil from your vessels.'" I am ashamed, I blush and I weep when I hear of a foolish virgin. When I hear that name I blush: after such virtue, after the practice of virginity, after giving the body wings toward heaven, after rivaling the powers above, after enduring the scorching heat, after trampling down the furnace of pleasure—then they were called foolish, and rightly foolish, because having accomplished the great thing, they were defeated by the small. "And the foolish came," it says… [Reg.: "which quickly opens the vaults… to men." Other notes, partly illegible: "…that is, even if you have many sins, but have almsgiving with you as advocate, do not fear; for none of the powers above opposes it…" [?] "Mercy triumphs over judgment," and "Redeem your sins by almsgiving" [?] "…of the least, you have done it to me…" [?] "it demands a debt, carrying its own bond…" [?] …the scorching heat [?] …foolish [?].]

…with his servants standing by, said to them: "Thank this man warmly on my behalf. He fed me and took me in when I was poor; he did me many kindnesses in my time of distress." Would not everyone spend all his money on the man whom the king thanked? Would he not count it well spent [?]? Would not everyone be eager to commend himself to him and become his friend?

3. Do you see the force of the argument? If such a thing brings so much honor in the case of a human king, think of Christ on that day calling out before the angels and every power and saying: "This man took me in on earth; this man did me countless kindnesses; this man welcomed me when I was a stranger." Think, then, of the confidence before the angels, the glory before the multitudes above. The one to whom Christ bears witness, how will he not have confidence beyond the angels? Almsgiving, then, is a great thing, brothers. Let us embrace it; nothing is equal to it. It is able to wipe out other sins and to drive away judgment. While you are silent, it stands and pleads for you; or rather, while you are silent, countless mouths give thanks on your behalf. Such great blessings come from almsgiving, and yet we are careless and slack. Give bread according to your means. You have no bread? Give an obol. You have no obol? Give a cup of cold water. You do not have that? Mourn with the afflicted, and you have a reward. For the reward is not for what necessity yields but for what the will chooses.

But while we have been talking about this, our concern with the virgins has slipped away. Come then, let us return to our subject. "Give us," it says, "oil from your vessels." "We cannot give it to you, in case there is not enough for us and for you. Go instead and buy from those who sell." While they were going away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those whose lamps were bright went in with him, and the door of the bridal chamber was shut. Then the five foolish ones also came and knocked at the door of the bridal chamber, crying, "Open to us!" And the voice of the bridegroom came to them from inside: "Go away from me; I do not know you." After so many labors, what did they hear? "I do not know you." This is what I was saying: they acquired the great possession of virginity in vain and to no purpose. Think of it: after so many labors they were cast out—when they had bridled incontinence, when they rivaled the powers above, when they laughed at the affairs of this life, when they endured the great scorching heat, when they leapt over the wrestling pits, when they rose on wings from earth to heaven, when they did not break the seal of the body, when they acquired the great form of virginity, when they rivaled the angels, when they trampled down the necessities of the body, when they forgot their nature, when in the body they accomplished what belongs to the bodiless, when they acquired the great and invincible possession of virginity—then they heard: "Go away from me; I do not know you." Do not suppose that the greatness of virginity is a small thing. Virginity is such that none of the ancients was able to keep it. That is why the grace is great, because [?] … in life; why do you gather money

4. But our discourse is a living thing, about the road of repentance and about almsgiving. We were saying that almsgiving is a great possession; from there the ocean of virginity took us over. You have, then, almsgiving as a first and great form of repentance, able to set you free from the chain of sins. But you also have another road of repentance, again very easy, by which to be rid of sins. Pray every hour, and do not lose heart in praying. Do not ask for God's love for mankind half-heartedly, and he will not turn away one who perseveres; he will forgive you your sins and grant your requests. If you are heard when you pray, continue giving thanks in prayer; if you were not heard, persevere in praying so that you may be heard. And do not say, "I prayed a great deal and was not heard." This often happens for your own good. He knows that you are careless and slack, and that if you obtain what you need, you will go away and pray no more. So he puts you off on account of your need, so that you may converse with God more often and give yourself to prayer. For if, being in such necessity and having such need, you are careless and do not persist in prayer, what would you do if you needed none of these things? So he does this for your benefit, wanting you not to abandon prayer. Persevere, then, in praying and do not be careless. Prayer can accomplish a great deal, beloved; do not approach prayer as if it were a small thing. That prayer forgives sins, learn from the divine Gospels. What does it say? "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who shut his door and lay down with his children. Someone came in the evening wanting to get loaves from him, and knocked, saying, 'Open to me, for I need loaves.' But he said to him, 'I cannot give to you now, for we have gone to bed, we and our children.' But the man kept knocking at the door. And he said to him again, 'I cannot give to you, for we have gone to bed, we and the children.' But even after hearing this, the man kept knocking and would not go away, until the master of the house said, 'Get up, give him what he wants, and let him go.'" He teaches us to pray always and never to grow weary, but, even if you do not receive, to persist until you do receive.

And you will find many other roads of repentance in Scripture. This repentance was proclaimed even before the coming of Christ through Jeremiah, who says: "Does the one who falls not rise, or the one who turns away not turn back?" And again: "After she had played the harlot, I said to her, Come, return to me." And for this reason he has given us many other different roads, to cut away every excuse for our carelessness. For if we had only one road, perhaps we could not enter by it [?]… this sword the devil always flees. Have you sinned? Come into the church and wipe out your sin. As often as you fall in the marketplace, so often you get up; in the same way, as often as you sin, repent of your sin. Do not despair of yourself. Even if you sin a second time, repent a second time, so that you do not, through carelessness, fall away completely from the hope of the good things set before us. Even if you sin in extreme old age, come in and repent. For this is a place of healing, not a court of judgment; it does not demand an account of sins, but grants forgiveness of sins [?]… [Illegible notes: "…he tells us… still… the road of repentance" [?].]

…and he himself grants you forgiveness of sins. You contribute some small occasion, so that your defense may look respectable. Some things come from him and some from us; if we contribute our part, he in turn supplies his own. He has already supplied his part: he established the sun, the moon, the varied choir of the stars; he poured out the air, spread out the earth, walled in the sea; he gave mountains, glens, hills, springs, lakes, rivers, the countless kinds of plants, gardens, and everything else. Now you in turn contribute a little, so that he may grant you the things above as well. Let us not, then, neglect ourselves or abandon our salvation, when we have so vast an ocean of love for mankind in the Master of all, who even grieves over our sins. The kingdom of heaven lies before us, and paradise, and the good things "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him." Ought we not to do everything to contribute something, so as not to lose these things? Or do you not know what Paul says—he who labored so much and set up countless trophies against the devil, who traveled the world on foot in the body, who ran over land and sea and air, who like one with wings [went round] the world… ON REPENTANCE AND PRAYER.

1. Shepherds keep leading their sheep to wherever they see the grass growing thickest, and do not move them from there until the flocks have cropped it all. We too, imitating them, have now for the fourth day been pasturing this flock on the subject of repentance, and even today we are not preparing to move it on, since we see that there is still plenty of pasture, and much delight as well as benefit. The foliage of trees, serving the sheep as a roof at midday, does not refresh them so much—providing welcome and healthful shade and lulling them to sleep with great pleasure—as the reading of the divine Scriptures restores and cools souls that are in pain and gripped by despondency, removing the fierce and burning heat of their pain and offering a comfort sweeter and more delightful than any shade. It gives us great comfort not only in losses of money, or in the deaths of children, or in other such things, but also in the crises brought on by sins. When a person is caught by sin, tripped up, and falls, and then his conscience eats away at him, constantly reminding him of the sin, so that he chokes himself with excessive despondency and is set on fire every day, and does not accept the comfort even though countless people console him—if he comes into the church and hears that many of the saints fell and rose again and returned to their former good standing, he goes away having received comfort without realizing it. With people, when we have sinned, we often cannot bring ourselves to reveal the offense, out of shame and embarrassment, and even if we do reveal it, [he] accepts nothing [Mumf., however, reads "προσείη"] [?]… from the sight alone; but with the soul it is not so,

rather the opposite happens: constantly thinking about those who have suffered such things makes our despondency over our own troubles lighter. That is why Paul too comforts the faithful in this way, bringing forward not only the saints who are living but also those who have died. When he addresses the Hebrews, who were about to be tripped up and fall, he brings forward the holy men—Daniel, the three young men, Elijah, Elisha—speaking like this: "They shut the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were stoned, experienced mockings and scourgings, and even chains and prison; they went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, men of whom the world was not worthy." Sharing in suffering gives comfort to those in pain. Just as suffering something terrible alone makes the evil comfortless, so finding another who has fallen into the same evils makes the blow lighter.

2. So that we may not collapse in all the things that seem to trouble us, let us pay careful attention to the stories of the Scriptures. From them we will gain a great resource for endurance, not only being comforted by fellowship with those who suffered the same things, but also learning the way of release from the troubles that come upon us, and, after relief, to remain in the same state, neither falling into carelessness nor being lifted up into arrogance. For it is nothing remarkable that people who are faring badly should be subdued and humbled and show great piety. The very nature of trials forces even those who have a heart of stone to do this—to be grieved. But it is the mark of a devout soul, one that keeps God always before its eyes, never to fall into forgetfulness even after release from trials. This is what the Jews constantly suffered. That is why the prophet mocked them, saying: "When he killed them, then they sought him, and turned back, and rose early to seek God." And Moses, knowing this very thing about them, constantly warned them, saying: "When you have eaten and drunk and are full, take heed to yourself, lest you forget the Lord your God." And this is exactly what happened: "Jacob ate," it says, "and grew fat and grew thick, and the beloved one kicked." So we should not admire the saints because they were so devout and wise while affliction was at its height, but because even when the storm had passed and calm had come, they remained in the same gentleness and zeal. And it is the horse that can walk in good order without a bridle that we should most admire; if it behaves well while muzzle and bridle restrain it, that is nothing remarkable, for its good conduct should be credited not to the animal's good breeding but to the compulsion of the bridle. The same can be said of the soul: that it is quiet while fear presses on it is nothing remarkable; but when the trials have passed and the bridle of fear has been removed, then show me the wisdom of the soul and all its good order. But I am afraid that in wanting to accuse the Jews I may be accusing our own way of life. For we too, when we were shaken by famine and plague and hail and [Savile: "of those who suffered."]

…[when the soul] is well disposed, whatever misfortune befalls, whether famine, or disease, or slander, or the plundering of property, or anything else at all, it will be bearable and light, because of the Master's commandment and our hope in him. In the same way, when the soul is not rightly disposed toward God, then even if wealth flows in, even if there are children, even if there is the enjoyment of countless riches, such a person will draw many griefs and cares upon himself. So let us not seek wealth or flee poverty. Above all, let each of us take care of his own soul and make it fit both for managing the present life and for the journey from here to there. For yet a little while, and each of us will be tested, when we all stand before the fearful judgment seat of Christ, clothed in our own deeds, and see with our own eyes the tears of orphans, the shameful debaucheries with which we defiled our souls, the groans of widows, the blows dealt to the poor, the robberies of the needy. And not only these and things like them, but anything improper we have done even in thought; for he is the Judge of thoughts and the critic of intentions, and again, he Searches hearts and minds, and Renders to each according to his work. These words of mine are addressed not only to those engaged in the life of the world, but also to those who have pitched their huts on the mountains for the sake of the monastic life. Such people ought to guard not only their bodies from the defilement of fornication, but also their soul from all satanic greed. For the apostle Paul speaks not only to women, but also to men and to the whole Church, when he says that the soul living in virginity must be holy in both body and spirit; and again, Present your bodies as a pure virgin. And pure in what way? Having no spot or wrinkle. For those virgins whose lamps had gone out were also virgins in body, but not pure in heart. Even if no man had corrupted them, the love of money had. Their body was pure, but their soul was full of much adultery: evil thoughts had entered them, love of money, mercilessness, anger, envy, idleness, forgetfulness and pride, and all of these ruined the dignity of their virginity. That is why Paul said, That the virgin may be holy in both body and spirit; and again, To present a pure virgin to Christ. For just as the body is corrupted by adulteries, so the [soul] is defiled by satanic thoughts, by corrupt doctrines, by improper notions. Whoever says, "I am a virgin in body," yet in his soul envies his brother, is not a virgin; the admixture of envy has corrupted his virginity. Again, the vainglorious man is not a virgin; the love of malice has corrupted his virginity, for the passion entered and dissolved the virginity of his soul. And whoever hates his brother is a murderer rather than a virgin. In short, whatever evil passion has a person in its grip, by that he corrupts his virginity. For this reason Paul banished all these evil things [?]… Have you told him your case? Have you told him what you have suffered? Then no longer say, "And how [will he help?]"; for he himself

knows exactly what is good for you. There are many who recite countless lines in the name of prayer, saying, "Lord, give me health of body, double my possessions, take vengeance on my enemy," and this is full of great folly. So we must leave all these things aside and only supplicate and plead like the tax collector who said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner; after that, he himself knows how to help you. For, he says, Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you. So, beloved, let us practise this wisdom with toil and humility, beating our breasts as he did, and we will obtain what we ask. But if we pray full of wrath and anger, we are found abominable and hateful before God. Let us therefore break our pride of mind and humble our souls, and pray both for ourselves and for those who have hurt us. For if you want to draw the judge to the help of your soul and win him to your side, never petition him against the one who has hurt you. This is the judge's way: he favours most and grants the requests of those who pray for their enemies, who bear no grudges, who do not rise up against [or: curse] their enemies. And the more these do so, the more God punishes those others, unless they turn and repent.

5. See to it, then, brothers: whenever someone brings some dishonour upon us, let us not at once be vexed and downcast, but give thanks, bearing it wisely and waiting for the Lord's help. Could God not have given us good things before we asked? Could he not have granted us a life without pain, free of every affliction? But he does both out of love. Why, then, does he allow us to be afflicted and not bring swift deliverance? Why? So that we may wait upon him, holding fast to the help that comes from him, and flee to him for refuge, and call on him continually to aid us. That is why there are bodily pains, why the crops fail, why there are famines: so that through these afflictions we may always hang upon him, and so, through temporary afflictions, inherit eternal life. So we ought to give thanks to God for these things too, since by many means he heals and saves our souls. For men, if they happen to do us a kindness at some point, and we then unintentionally hurt them a little, at once reproach us and throw the kindness in our face, as if many [?]… [?: variant reading "cursing".]

By the same author: a homily on fasting, and on the prophet Jonah, and on Daniel, and on the three youths. Delivered at the beginning of the holy fast.

Homily 5. 1. Bright is our festival today, and our assembly more splendid than usual. What, then, is the cause? This is the achievement of fasting, I know it well; of fasting not yet present, but expected. [?] …how much reverence will it produce in us? So too a city, when a fearful governor is about to enter, … all [?]. It is fasting that has gathered us into our fathers' house; it is fasting that has also [roused] those who before this

[lays a]side carelessness and settles into greater diligence. But do not cower when you hear that fasting is a fearful governor [?and a toilsome life]; for it is fearful not to us but to the nature of demons. If someone is possessed, show him the face of fasting, and he becomes more motionless than the very stones, frozen with fear as if held by a chain, and especially when he sees joined with fasting its sister and yokefellow, prayer. That is why Christ says, This kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting. Since, then, fasting drives off the enemies of our salvation in this way, and is so fearful to the enemies of our life, we ought to love and embrace it, not dread it. If we must fear anything, it is drunkenness and gluttony we should fear, not fasting. For they bind our hands behind our backs and hand us over as slaves and captives to the tyranny of the passions, as to a cruel mistress; but fasting, finding us enslaved and bound, releases us from our bonds, frees us from that tyranny, and leads us back to our former freedom. When, then, it both makes war on our enemies, and frees us from slavery, and restores us to freedom, what greater proof do you seek of its friendship toward our race? For the greatest proof of friendship is thought to be loving and hating the same things as we do. Do you want to learn how great an adornment fasting is to human beings, how great a guard and safeguard? Consider, I beg you, the blessed and wonderful race of monks. These men fled the tumults of the world, ran up to the mountain peaks, pitched their huts in the stillness of the desert as in a calm harbour, and took fasting as the companion and partner of their whole life. That is why it made them angels instead of men. And not only them: in the cities too, whomever it finds welcoming it, it leads up to the very height of the wise life. For Moses and Elijah, the towers among the prophets of the Old Testament, though they were brilliant and great for other reasons too and had great boldness before God, took refuge in fasting when they wished to approach God and converse with him, as far as was possible for a human being, and they were presented to him by its hands. That is why God too, when he made man in the beginning, at once handed him over into the hands of fasting, entrusting his salvation to it as to a loving mother and an excellent teacher. For the words, From every tree of paradise you shall eat for food, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, are a form of fasting. And if fasting was necessary in paradise, much more is it necessary outside paradise; if the medicine was useful before the wound, much more after the wound; if the weapon was suitable for us before the war of the desires had broken out, much more, after so great a battle against the desires and against the demons, is the alliance of fasting necessary. If Adam had listened to this voice, he would not have heard the second one, which says, Earth you are, and to earth you shall return. But because he disobeyed it, there came death and cares and toils and griefs and a life heavier than any death. Because of [?]… [?: one Regius manuscript reads] "of the one in paradise." …having love toward [?]. For, Peter,

he says, do you love me more than these? Nothing could equal this as a measure of virtue. So that you may not say that he was right to pardon the Ninevites, being barbarous and foolish men—for, he says, the servant who does not know his master's will and does not do it will be beaten with few blows—so that you may not say this, he has brought Peter before you, a servant who knew his master's will better than anyone. And yet even he, after sinning, and sinning the gravest sin, see to what height of boldness

So do not you yourself despair over your sins either. For what is worse than sinning is remaining in sin, and what is more terrible than falling is lying where you have fallen. This is what Paul laments and bewails; this, he says, deserves mourning. For I fear, he says, that when I come to you, God may humble me, and I may mourn over many—not over those who have simply sinned, but over those who have not repented of the debauchery and impurity and fornication they have practised. And what time could be more suitable for repentance than the time of fasting?

3. But let us return to the story. Having heard these words, the prophet went down to Joppa to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. Where are you fleeing, man? Have you not heard the prophet saying, Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? To the earth? But The earth is the Lord's, and all that fills it. To Hades? If I go down into Hades, he says, you are there. To heaven? But if I go up to heaven, you are there. To the sea? Even there, he says, your right hand will hold me. And this is just what happened in his case. But such is sin: it throws our soul into great folly. For just as people seized by a heavy head and drunkenness are carried about aimlessly and at random, and whether a pit or a cliff or anything else lies before them, they fall into it without taking care, so too those who slip into sin, seized by desire for the deed as by a kind of drunkenness, do not know what they are doing; they foresee nothing either of the present or of the future. You are fleeing the Master, tell me? Then wait a little, and you will learn from the events themselves that you cannot escape even the hands of the sea, his servant. For no sooner had he boarded the ship than the sea raised up its waves and swelled to a great height. And just as a loyal maidservant, finding a fellow slave who has run away after stealing some of the master's property, does not let up, causing endless trouble to those who have taken him in, until she seizes him and leaves, so too the sea, finding and recognizing its fellow slave, causes endless trouble to the sailors, churning, roaring, not dragging them to court, but threatening to sink the vessel with all hands unless they hand over its fellow slave. What, then, did the sailors do when this happened? They threw overboard, it says, the gear that was in the ship; but the ship was not lightened. For the whole cargo still remained inside: the prophet's body, that heavy burden, heavy not because of the body's nature but because of the weight of sin. For nothing is so heavy and hard to bear [?]…

since these men do not despise even one soul, but [?: …did not touch him, though… nature itself rousing them (for nothing is fiercer than those beasts…)] spare a single body, yours; whereas you, for your part, gave up a whole city with so many tens of thousands. And they, though they had found the cause of the evils that had come upon them, did not even then rush to a verdict of condemnation; but you, having nothing to charge against the Ninevites, sank and destroyed them. And you, when I ordered you to go and call them to salvation by your preaching, did not obey; but these men, though no one told them, do everything and take every pains to rescue you, who had become liable to punishment. For indeed, even after the accusation brought by the sea, after the proof given by the lot, when he accused himself and confessed his flight, not even then did they rush to destroy the prophet. They held back and strained at the oars and did everything they could so as not to hand him over to the onslaught of the sea even after such proof. But not even so did the sea allow it; or rather, God did not allow it, wishing to bring him to his senses through the sea monster as he had through the sailors. For after hearing, Pick me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will calm down for you, they strove hard to reach land, but the waves would not allow it.

4. Now, just as you have seen the prophet fleeing, hear him also confessing from down below, from the belly of the beast. The first he suffered as a man; the second he displayed as a prophet. The sea, then, took him and placed him in the belly of the sea monster as in a prison, keeping the fugitive safe for the Master. The savage waves did not drown him when they took him, nor did the monster, more savage than the waves, destroy him when it received him into its belly; it kept him safe and brought him back to the city. Sea and monster obeyed against their nature, so that the prophet might be taught by every means. Coming then to the city, he read out the sentence like a royal letter announcing punishment, and cried out, saying, Three days more, and Nineveh will be overthrown. They heard it; they did not disbelieve, they did not scoff, but at once everyone ran to fasting: men, women, slaves, masters, rulers, subjects, children, elders. Not even the irrational animals were exempt from this service. Everywhere sackcloth, everywhere ashes, everywhere lamentation and wailing. For even the one who wore the diadem came down from his royal throne, spread sackcloth beneath him, sprinkled himself with ashes, and so snatched the city from danger. A paradox: the purple [saved] by sackcloth! What the purple could not do, the sackcloth [?accomplished]; what the diadem did not achieve, the ashes accomplished. Do you see that I did not speak idly when I said that it is not fasting we should fear, but drunkenness and gluttony? For drunkenness and gluttony shook the city while it still stood and were about to throw it down, but fasting set it firm again when it was tottering and about to fall. With fasting Daniel too went into the lions' den and, after being among the wild beasts, came out unharmed. For [?]… seething with rage and with murder in their eyes, … of the table [?]…

[?]… you made it [useless] and profitless; you endured the toil but did not reap the gain of it, since the fresh wickedness arising from drunkenness consumes all its power. But if you make your body light for it and receive the medicine with a sober mind, you will be able to wash away many of your old sins. So let us not come to the fast by way of drunkenness, nor break off the fast again in drunkenness, lest it be like someone who kicks a sick body just as it is about to get up and throws it down again more violently. That is what happens to our soul when, on both sides, at the beginning and at the end of the fast, we overcast with the cloud of drunkenness the sobriety we have gained from abstinence. For just as those about to fight wild beasts fence in the vital parts of their limbs with many weapons and protections and only then take on the fight with them, so too now there are many people who, as though about to fight fasting as if it were a wild beast, arm themselves with gluttony in this way, and having stuffed themselves to bursting and darkened their minds, receive in great madness the calm and gentle face of fasting. And if I ask you, "Why are you running to the bath today?" "So that with a clean body [I may begin] the fast [?]…" …for ever and ever. Amen. [?: one manuscript lacks "of the holy"; Savile reads "of the presiding (bishops)".]

Homily on fasting, delivered in the sixth week of holy Lent.

1. How delightful are the waves of this spiritual sea of ours, more delightful even than those of the open sea! The disorder of the winds raises those, but the desire to hear raises these. Those, when they crest, cause the helmsman great anxiety, but these, when they appear, give the speaker great confidence. Those are signs of a storm-tossed sea, but these are signs of a soul that rejoices. Those, dashing against the rocks, give out a meaningless roar, but these, breaking against the word of teaching, give out a gentle voice. So too, when the breezes of the west wind fall upon the cornfields and bend and lift the heads of the ears, they imitate the waves of the sea on dry land. But these are more delightful even than those cornfields; for it is not the breezes of the west wind but the grace of the Spirit that has stirred and warmed your souls. And that fire of which Christ once said, I came to cast fire on the earth, and what more do I wish, if it is already kindled?—that fire I see cast down and burning in your souls. Since, then, the fear of Christ has lit so many lamps for us, come, let us drop upon them from here the oil of teaching, so that the light may last longer for us. For the season of fasting is now hastening to its end; having reached the middle of the course, we are now drawing near the finish. For just as one who begins [?reaches] the middle, so one who has come to the middle has laid hold of the end. The season, then, toward the end… [?: one manuscript's title reads "On holy Lent, on fasting"; the Ottoboni manuscript reads "raise".]

[?]…that place, full of every kind of disease, [318] the Babylonian furnace. For the devil has thrown the city into the theater as into a furnace, and he stokes it from below. He does not pile on brushwood, as that barbarian did long ago, nor naphtha, nor tow, nor pitch, but things far worse than these: the looks of harlots, shameful words, mincing limbs, songs full of every kind of wickedness. Barbarian hands lit that furnace, but this furnace is lit by thoughts more senseless than any barbarian's. This one is worse than that, because its fire is worse: it does not burn the body's substance but ruins the health of the soul. And what is worse still, those who are burning do not even feel it. If they felt it, they would not burst into loud laughter at what goes on there. This is the worst thing of all: when a sick man does not even know that he is sick, and while burning wretchedly and miserably does not feel the flames. What good is fasting when you keep your body from its customary food but feed your soul on lawless food? When you spend the whole day sitting there, watching our common nature disgraced and held up to public shame: women playing the harlot, men acting out adulteries, people gathering up the evils of every household? For there you can see fornications and adulteries and hear blasphemies, so that the disease enters the soul through both eyes and ears. They imitate other people's calamities, and that is why the name of shame attaches to them. What then is the gain of fasting when the soul is fed on such things? With what eyes will you look at your wife after those shows? With what eyes will you look at your son, your servant, your friend? Anyone who tells what goes on there must either disgrace himself or keep silent and shrink away, blushing. But you do not leave here like that. At home you will be able to recount with complete freedom everything that is said here: the voices of the prophets, the teachings of the apostles, the laws of the Lord, and so set out the whole table of virtue. With the stories you bring from here you make your wife more chaste, your son wiser, your servant more loyal, your friend more friendly, and you even persuade your enemy himself to lay down his enmity.

2. Do you see how these teachings bring salvation everywhere, while those shows are useless everywhere? So what good is fasting, tell me, when you fast with your body but commit adultery with your eyes? For adultery is not only intercourse or bodily union; it is also a licentious look. What good is it when you come here and go there as well? I teach, he corrupts. I apply remedies to the disease, he feeds the disease. I quench the flame of nature, he kindles the flame of desire. What good is it, tell me? "When one builds and another tears down, what have they gained but toil?" So let us not spend our time both here and there, but here only, so that our time here may be profitable, not in vain, not to no purpose, and not to our condemnation. "When one builds and another tears down, what have they gained but [519] toil?" And yet even if many… [Notes: From "Babylonian" to "worse" [?]… in the editions [?]. In Barocc. [?], and in the translator [?]. "τούς" is missing; but Ottob. has "ἐκείνους". [?] "ὀφθαλμοῖς". Both mss.: "ἀνέστειλεν".]

…when he says, "For our momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure." What he says is a riddle. If it is affliction, how is it light? If it is light, how is it affliction? These are opposites. But he solved the riddle with what follows, showing how it is light. How? "Because we look not at the things that are seen." He set out the crown and made the contest light; he displayed the prize and gave comfort for the sweat. So you too, when you see a woman radiant in her looks and splendid in her dress, when you feel desire tickling you and your soul longing to gaze, look up to the crown laid up for you above, so that you may run past such a sight. Have you seen a fellow servant? Think of the Master, and you will surely put an end to the disease. If children who follow their tutor do not turn around, do not gape, do not get flustered, much more will you be untouched by anything of the kind if you see Christ present in your thoughts. "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." I read the words of the law gladly and often. I wish I could say this to you all day long, or rather not to you but to those who are guilty of these sins; or rather to you too. You will be safer, and those who are in the grip of the disease will quickly return to health. "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." 3. These words, simply read aloud, are enough to cleanse all the rot of sin. But forgive me: we are cleaning wounds, and whoever cleans wounds must also apply bitter remedies. The more you bear with these words, the more the corrosion is cleansed away. Fire, the longer it stays in contact with gold, the more it eats away the tarnish. In the same way the fear these words inspire, the longer it resounds in your minds, the more completely it will cleanse away all the sin of licentiousness. Let us burn the soul here with the word of teaching, so that we may not be forced to burn it there with the fire of Gehenna. The soul that departs from here pure will not be harmed at all by that fire, but the soul that departs from here with its sins, that fire will receive. "For the fire," it says, "will test what sort of work each one has done." Let us test ourselves now without pain, so that we may not be tested then with pain. [321] "Say what you like," someone says, "the law is burdensome." What then? Does God command us to do the impossible? I do not say so. Bridle your tongue, do not accuse the Master. That is no way to defend yourself; it only adds a sin worse than the first. Hear how it is the habit of many sinners to throw the blame on the Master. The man who had been entrusted with five talents came forward and brought five more. The man who had been entrusted with two talents came forward and brought two more. The man who had been entrusted with one talent came forward, and since another… [Notes: Both: "how affliction". Shortly after, both omit the following "light" together with "τῆς" [?]. "How then is it light, how [?]". Both mss.: "γαργαλίζουσιν"; editions: "γαργαλιζομένην". Below [?]. Ottob.: "πλέον". And shortly after, the same: "and in the case of the words". [?]: "Speak no ill, and bridle your tongue", not a bad reading. Ottob.: "and I exhort [?]".]

…to make full use of my authority. There it was law, and so it did not carry a great reward; but this was a matter of free choice, and so it earned a great reward. 4. I have not said all this idly, but for the sake of the divine law, to show that it is not heavy, not burdensome, not toilsome, and not impossible. Come, let us make this very point clear from Christ's own words: "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." Christ too foresaw this very thing, that many would accuse the law of being difficult. That is why he did not introduce it bare and unadorned, on its own, but also reminds them of the old law, using the comparison to show both how easy his law is and how great his love for humankind. Pay attention to how he does it. He did not simply say, "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (here attend carefully). First he reminded them of the old law, saying: "You have heard that it was said to those of old, You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you, everyone who looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." You have seen the two laws, the old and the new: the one Moses laid down, and the one he himself introduces. Or rather, he himself laid down the old one as well, for he spoke through Moses. And how is it clear that he laid down that one too? I will not bring testimony from John or from the apostles, since my contest now is with the Jews. I will prove from the prophets, whom they profess to believe, that the Old and the New have one lawgiver. What then does Jeremiah say? "I will make a new covenant with you." Do you see the name of the New even in the Old? Do you see its very title shining out so many ages beforehand? "I will make a new covenant with you." But how is it clear that he also gave the Old? Having said, "I will make a new covenant with you," he added, "not like the covenant that I made with your fathers." Yes, but we have not yet proved the point. We must bring every objection into the open and deal with it plainly, so that our argument may be clear on every side and no excuse may be left even to the shameless. "I will make a new covenant with you, not like the covenant that I made with your fathers." He made a covenant [525] with Noah when the flood took place, wishing to free us from our fears, so that when we saw floods and kept seeing rain we would not expect that universal destruction to come again. That is why he says, "I will make a covenant with you and with all flesh." Again, he made with Abraham the covenant of circumcision; and he made a covenant through Moses, the one known to everyone. Jeremiah said: "I will make a new covenant with you, not like the covenant that I made with your fathers." Tell me, which fathers? Noah was a father, and Abraham was a father. Which fathers does he mean, then? For leaving the persons unspecified creates confusion. Pay attention here: "Not like the covenant that I made with your fathers." So that you could not say he means the covenant made in Noah's time, or the one made in Abraham's time, he went on to mention the actual time of the covenants, like this: having said, "I will make a new co[venant] with you…" [Notes: [?]… Ottob.: "ἐνεθίζων".]

…the prophecy by deed? For having wives is not a word but a deed. I have shown you the slave woman and the free woman through words, proving that the two covenants have one lawgiver; now learn the same thing through the types as well. Abraham had two wives; these are the two covenants, and there is one lawgiver. Just as there we had a sheep and a sheep, one in word and the other in deed, and the agreement between deeds and words was complete, so here too there are two covenants: Jeremiah foretold them in words, and Abraham prefigured them in deeds by having two wives. As there is one husband and two wives, so there is one lawgiver and two covenants. But to return to what I was saying, the point that set all this in motion (for we must not lose the thread of our subject): "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." Yes; but, and this is why we raised all these matters, why does he read the old law to them? For he says to them, "You have heard that it was said to those of old, You shall not commit adultery." He knew that the command is difficult, not by its own nature but because of the laziness of those who hear it. Many things that are easy by nature become hard to accomplish when we are lazy, just as things that are difficult become light and very easy when we are earnest. The difficulty does not lie in the nature of things but in the will of those who undertake them. That this is true is clear from the following. Honey is by nature sweet and most pleasant, yet to the sick it is bitter and unpleasant, not because of its own nature but because of their illness. So too the law, if it seems burdensome, seems so not because of its own nature but because of our laziness. It takes me no great effort to show that it is easy to keep, for what would have made it difficult would have been to say the opposite. As it is, he says, "Flee the sight of a woman, keep away from licentiousness." The hard thing would have been to say the opposite: "Study women closely, pry into the beauty of other men's wives, and master your desire that way." That would indeed have been difficult. But for him to say, "Flee the furnace, stand away from the fire, do not go near the flame, so that you may remain unharmed," makes it very easy, for [525] the command is in accord with nature. "You have heard that it was said to those of old, You shall not commit adultery." Why then does he remind us of the old law when he is about to introduce another? So that you may learn from the comparison that there is no conflict between the one and the other. When there is a comparison, the judgment becomes clearer. Since some were going to accuse him of saying these things as legislation against the old law, he says: "See, I set the two laws side by side; examine them and learn how they agree." And not only for this reason, but also to show that his law is easy and introduced at the right time. That is why he says, "You have heard that it was said to those of old, You shall not commit adultery": you have practiced the old law for so long. A teacher speaking to a lazy child who wants to linger still over old lessons, and wishing to lead him up to higher things, says, "Think how long you have been stuck on this lesson." In the same way Christ too reminds them that they have practiced and held to the old law for a long time, and that it is now time to go up to the higher one, into… [Notes: [?] "for the sake of"; I would gladly read "τοῦτο" in place of "τούτου". [?] Ottob. and Barocc.: "τοῖς παλαιοις". Ottob. and Barocc.: "τοῖς παλαιοῖς".]

…keeping this in mind, and remembering what we have said about licentiousness and how great a punishment awaits those who look casually and licentiously at women's faces, and keeping before our eyes, even more than Gehenna, the fear and the love of God, let us cleanse ourselves on every side and so approach the holy mysteries, so that not to judgment…
A DISCOURSE ON REPENTANCE and compunction, and that God is quick to save and slow to punish; in which is also the remarkable story of Rahab.

1. The divine Apostle always speaks with a divine and heavenly tongue, and weaves the message of the Gospel with great skill. He does not simply speak his own mind; he brings forth his teachings with royal authority. He uses this skill above all when he brings the message of repentance to sinners, and it is on this very point that I want to remind you all. You heard just now, to touch on part of what was read, how that noble and wonderful man said when addressing the Corinthians: "Lest when I come I may have to mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented." This great teacher was a man by nature, but a servant of God by his purpose. That is why he uses, as it were, a heavenly tongue, and as though speaking from heaven itself he threatens sinners and promises atonement to those who repent. [?] When I say this, I will not attribute the authority to Paul's tongue but refer it all to the grace of God, of which he himself has just said, "Since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me." So he offers sinners a remedy of kindness, and repentance leading to salvation. And today the Savior's authority in the Gospel joined with the reading from the Apostle, granting forgiveness of sins without stint. For as you have just heard, when the Savior healed the paralytic he said, "Child, your many sins are forgiven you." Forgiveness of sins is a fountain of salvation and the prize of repentance. Repentance is a remedy that destroys sin; it is a heavenly gift, a wonderful power that by grace overcomes the strict logic of the laws. That is why it does not shake off the fornicator, does not drive away the adulterer, does not turn its back on the drunkard, does not loathe the idolater, does not expel the reviler, does not chase away the blasphemer or the boaster, but transforms them all; for repentance is a furnace that melts down sin. But first we must know God's purpose, not approaching this inquiry with our own notions but demonstrating the truth as it is attested in the divine Scriptures themselves. God's purpose in being patient with sinners is twofold, and gracious, leading to salvation: he woos for them the salvation that comes through repentance, and for their descendants, who will go on to advance in virtue, he stores up the… [Notes: One Reg.: "it receives all and transforms all; for repentance is a furnace that refines virtue." One Reg.: "evangelical".]

…the same account of his love for humankind holds for these too. If punishment had come before correction, the world would have perished and been destroyed altogether. If God were quick to punish, the Church would not have gained Paul; it would not have received so great a man. That is why he held off from punishing him while he blasphemed, so that he might show him repenting. God's patience made the persecutor a herald. God's patience turned the wolf into a shepherd. God's patience made the tax collector an evangelist. God's patience has had mercy on us all, changed us all, turned us all around. If you see someone who was once a drunkard now fasting, if you see someone who was once a blasphemer now a theologian, if you see someone who once defiled his mouth with shameful songs now cleansing his soul with divine hymns, marvel at God's patience, praise repentance, and taking your cue from the change, say: "This change is the work of the right hand of the Most High." God is good to all, but he shows his patience especially toward sinners. And if you want to hear a strange saying, strange to ordinary habits but true to piety, listen. God everywhere appears stern toward the righteous but kind toward sinners and quick to show love. He raises up the one who has sinned and fallen, and says to him: "Does not one who falls get up again? Does not one who turns away turn back?" And: "Why has the foolish daughter of Judah turned away in shameless backsliding?" And again: "Turn to me, and I will turn to you." And elsewhere, in his great love, he confirms with an oath the salvation that comes through repentance: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live." But to the righteous he says: "If a man does all righteousness and all truth, and then turns away and sins, I will not remember his righteousness, but he shall die in his sin." What great strictness toward the righteous! What great generosity toward the sinner! He works in these various and different ways not because he himself changes, but because he distributes the dispensations of his goodness as each case requires. Hear how. If he frightens the sinner who persists in his sins, he drives him to despair and the abandonment of hope. If he calls the righteous man blessed, he slackens [529] the tension of his virtue and makes him neglect his efforts, as though he had already been declared blessed. That is why he has mercy on the sinner but frightens the righteous: "For he is fearsome to all who are around him," and "The Lord is good to all." "He is fearsome," it says, "to all who are around him"; and who could these be but the saints? "For God," says David, "who is glorified in the council of the saints, is great and fearsome to all who are around him." If he sees someone fallen, he stretches out the hand of love; if he sees someone standing, he brings fear to bear; and this belongs to justice and righteous judgment. For he will steady the righteous by fear and rouse the sinner by love. Do you want to know his timely goodness, and the severity that is useful and suited to us? Pay close attention, so that the greatness of what we are considering does not escape you. That sinful woman… [Notes: One Reg.: "he brings fear to bear, as belongs to justice and righteous judgment, steadying the one by fear and raising up the other by love." One Reg.: "to the table".]

[?] of piety. So he pities sinners as poor, and makes demands of those who do right as rich. To the first he shows favour because of their poverty; from the second, because of their wealth of piety, he exacts the account with great strictness. And what he does with the righteous and with sinners, he also does with the rich and the poor. Just as he raises up the sinner out of his love for humankind but makes the righteous man fear by his severity, so too he arranges his dispensation in worldly affairs. If he sees men of power who shine with high rank, such as kings, rulers and all who are distinguished by wealth, he speaks to them with fear, and he usefully lays fear upon their power: “Now therefore, O kings, understand; be instructed, all you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling,” for he is King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule. Where there is the rule of power, he lays upon it the fear of his own kingship; where there is the humility of lowliness, he applies the medicine of his love for humankind.
