For this God, the great King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule, is the same one who again steps down from his own dignity and is found, according to the holy Scripture, to be father of orphans and judge of widows, as well as King of kings, Ruler of rulers and Lord of lords. Do you see the great abundance of his love for humankind? Do you see how useful the fear of piety and of authority is? Where he saw that authority was enough to give comfort, he imposed fear for their benefit. But where he saw orphanhood crippled by lowliness, and poverty crippled by the helplessness of widowhood, he brought his love for humankind to comfort them. “I am father of orphans.” He does two things: he displays his love for humankind and he chastens power. He calls himself father of orphans to comfort those in misfortune and to strike terror into those in power, so that they will not abuse orphans and widows. Death stripped the one of his father and bereft the other of her husband, and those whom the law of nature had ruined, the decree of love for humankind renewed. This new grace gave the widow a judge and the orphan a father, the King of the saints. “So,” he says, “you unjust man, if you abuse widows, you provoke the guardian of widows; if you wrong orphans, you wrong sons of God. I am the father of orphans and the judge of widows.” And who is so bold in impiety that he would wrong sons of God and abuse widows whom God cares for? Do you see how usefully he prepares the medicines of piety? He frightens some and pities others, not because he is divided in himself, but because he adapts himself to people's dispositions. So let us apply repentance to ourselves, brothers, as a medicine for salvation. Or rather, let us receive from God the repentance that heals us. For it is not we who bring it to him; he is the one who supplied it to us. Do you see his strictness in the law? Do you see his love for humankind in grace? When I speak of the strictness in the law, I am not maligning [?]; rather, I am proclaiming the love for humankind of the grace of the gospel. For the law punished sinners without pardon, but grace patiently postpones punishment in order to bring about correction. So let us accept repentance, brothers, as a medicine for salvation; let us accept a medicine that wipes out our [?]

[?] of sins blinding the soul of sinners, because the ears of those plunged in the depth of sin have become deaf. So he holds back from applying help while the passion is still inflamed, and only after a long time does the reproof come. Then, in a single moment, come repentance and forgiveness: “And the Lord has put away your sin.” O the dispensation of the one who threatened! Do you see that he is swift to save? He does this in other matters as well: he is slow to destroy but quick to help. Here is what I mean. Among us humans, buildings are put up over a long period, and it takes us a long time to build a house; building takes much time, demolition little. With God it is the reverse. When he builds, he builds swiftly; when he overthrows, he overthrows slowly. God is swift in creating and slow in destroying, since both befit God: the one belongs to power, the other to goodness. He is swift because his power surpasses all, and slow because his goodness is great. The facts themselves prove the words. In six days God made the heaven and the earth, the great mountains, the plains, the ravines, the glens, the forests, the plants, springs, rivers, paradise and all the visible variety of things. He made this great and wide sea, the islands, and the lands along the coast and inland. All this visible world and the beauty in it God made in six days; the living creatures in it, rational and irrational, and all the visible order he makes in six days. Yet this God who is so swift to create was found slow, out of goodness, when he resolved to destroy a single city. He wants to destroy Jericho, and he says to Israel: “March around it for seven days, and on the seventh day the wall will fall.” You construct the whole world in six days, and you take seven days to undo one city? What hinders your power? Why not destroy it all at once? Is it not about you that the prophet cries out, “If you open heaven, trembling will seize the mountains at your presence, and they will melt like wax before fire”? Does not David, recounting the works of your power, say, “We will not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the seas”? You can move mountains and cast them into the sea, yet you will not destroy one city that resists you, but give seven days to its destruction? Why? “It is not that my power is weak,” he says, “but that my love for humankind is patient. I give seven days, as I gave Nineveh three; perhaps it will receive the preaching of repentance and be saved.” And who was preaching repentance to them? Enemies had besieged the city; the general was marching around the walls; there was great fear and great tumult. What way of repentance, then, did you open to them? Did you send a prophet? Did you dispatch an evangelist? Was there anyone to show them what was good for them? “Yes,” he says, “they had a teacher of repentance inside the city, that wonderful Rahab, whom I saved through repentance.” She was of the same lump as they were. But since she was not of the same mind, she who had not shared their unbelief did not share their sin. 5. And see, I pray you, the strange proclamation of love for humankind: the one who says in the law, “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not fornicate,” [?] [? and Savile: “had surrounded”].

[?] and preserved. So Rahab, the image of the Church, is worthy of all praise. That is why the noble Paul also recognized the worth of her faith. He did not consider her disqualified because of her former condition, but approved because of her divine change, and so he numbers her among all the saints. Having said, “By faith Abel offered a sacrifice; by faith Abraham did this and that; by faith Noah built an ark; by faith Moses did and accomplished this and that,” and having mentioned many saints in turn, he added last of all: “By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with those who disobeyed, because she received the spies and sent them out by another way.” And see how wisely she blended her good sense. When men were sent by the king to look for the spies, they said to her, “Did men come in to you?” And she said to them, “Yes, they came.” First she builds up the truth, and then she adds the lie. For a lie is never believed on its own unless it first displays some truth. That is why those who lie persuasively first say what is true and agreed by everyone, and only then add what is false and disputed. “Did spies come in to you?” She says, “Yes.” If she had said “No” from the start, she would have invited the men who had come to search the house. Instead she says, “They came in, and they went out by this road; pursue them and you will catch them.” O good lie! O good deceit, which does not betray divine things but guards piety! Repentance made that Rahab worthy of so great a salvation, and she is proclaimed by the mouths of saints: Joshua son of Nun cried out in the desert, “Let Rahab the harlot live,” and Paul said, “By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with those who disobeyed.” If that is so, how much more will we receive salvation if we offer repentance? The present time is a time for repentance, for the sins that weigh on us give great cause for fear, unless repentance comes before the punishment. “Let us come before his presence with confession.” Let us quench the blaze of our sins, not with much water but with a few tears. The fire of sin is great, and yet it is quenched by a little tear; for a tear quenches the blaze of sins and washes away the stench of sin. The blessed David bears witness to this and shows how great the power of tears is: “Every night,” he says, “I will wash my bed; with my tears I will drench my couch.” Yet if he had wanted only to show how abundant his tears were, it would have been enough to say, “With my tears I will drench my couch.” Why then did he put “I will wash” first? To show that tears are a bath and a cleansing of sins. 6. Sins are the cause of all evils. Because of sins come griefs, because of sins disturbances, because of sins wars, because of sins diseases, and all the afflictions that befall us and are hard to cure. The best physicians do not just examine the ailments that are visible but look for the cause of what appears. In the same way the Savior wished to show that sin is the cause of all the evils among humans. He, the physician of souls, saw that the man paralyzed in body had first been paralyzed in soul and only then in body, and so he said to him: “See, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.” So sin was the cause of the earlier illness too. It is also the cause of loss, of grief, of calamity

[?] the recompense. Here righteousness is bought for little: for a cheap scrap of bread, a cheap garment, a cup of cold water. “Whoever gives a cup of cold water to drink, truly I tell you,” says the teacher of spiritual commerce, “will not lose his reward.” A cup of cold water earns a reward; do garments and money given in kindness not earn one? On the contrary, they earn a great reward. Why then did he mention a cup of cold water? He was speaking of almsgiving that costs nothing, for with cold water you use up no firewood and spend nothing else. If the grace of the good deed is so great where the gift costs nothing, how great a reward must we expect from the just Judge where there are plenty of garments, a supply of money and an abundance of other goods? So while the virtues are on display and sold for little, let us take them from the generous Giver; let us seize them, let us buy them. “You who thirst,” he says, “come to the water, and you who have no money, go and buy.” While the fair is on, let us buy almsgiving, or rather, let us buy salvation through almsgiving. When you clothe a poor man, you clothe Christ. “I know this well and exactly,” someone says. “I learned it long ago. You are not the first to teach it; we have not heard it first from you. You are not preaching anything new, but what many of those here have often taught us.” I know it myself, I know that you have often learned these things and others like them. But I wish that, having learned them so often, we might do even a little good. “Whoever has mercy on a poor man lends to God.” Let us lend our almsgiving to God, so that we may receive from him the return of his love for humankind. But how wise this saying is! “Whoever has mercy on a poor man lends to God.” Why did it not say, “Whoever has mercy on a poor man gives to God,” but rather “lends”? Scripture knows our greed. It noticed that our insatiable appetite looks to gain and seeks interest. That is why it did not simply say, “Whoever has mercy on a poor man gives to God,” so that you would not think the recompense was merely equal. Instead it says, “Whoever has mercy on a poor man lends to God.” If God borrows from us, then he is our debtor. Which would you rather have him be, then, judge or debtor? A debtor respects his lender; a judge is not swayed by the borrower. 7. But we must also consider in another way why God said, “The one who gives to the poor lends to me.” He saw our greed leaning toward profit, as I said before. He saw that no one with money is willing to lend without security. A lender demands a mortgage, or pledges, or a guarantor, and he entrusts his money on these three securities: sureties, as I said, or a mortgage on property, or pledges. So God saw that apart from these no one lends, and no one looks to kindness but only to gain. He saw that the poor man lacks all of these. He has no mortgage to offer, for he owns nothing; he brings no pledges, for he has been stripped bare; he offers no guarantor, for he is distrusted because of his destitution. When God saw the poor man in danger from his destitution, and the man with money in danger because of his inhumanity, he placed himself between them, as a surety for the poor man and a pledge for the lender. “You do not trust this man because of his destitution,” he says; “trust me because of my abundance.” He saw the poor man and had pity; he saw the poor man and did not overlook him, but gave himself as a pledge for the one who has nothing [?]

[?] he says, “and you clothed me.” We clothed the one who clothes the heaven with clouds, who clothes the whole Church and the whole world. “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” “I was in prison.” You in prison, who lead out those in chains? Explain what you are saying, for your dignity contradicts your words. “When did we see you in such want? When did we do these things?” “Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these,” he says, “you did it to me.” Is it not true, then, that “Whoever has mercy on a poor man lends to God”? And notice something remarkable: he mentioned no other work of virtue but this one. He could have said, “Come, you blessed, because you were chaste, because you kept your virginity, because you took up the angelic way of life.” But he says nothing of these things, not because they are unworthy of mention, but because they come second to love for humankind. Just as he showed those on the right that the kingdom was granted to them because of their love for humankind, so he threatened those on the left with punishment because of their fruitlessness: “Go, you cursed, into the outer darkness prepared for the devil and his angels.” Why? For what reason? “Because I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat.” He did not say, “Because you fornicated, because you committed adultery, because you stole, because you bore false witness, because you perjured yourselves.” These too are admittedly evils, but they are less serious than inhumanity and lack of mercy. Why, Lord, do you not mention other paths? “I do not judge sin,” he says, “but inhumanity. I do not judge those who sinned, but those who did not repent. I condemn you for your inhumanity, because you had so great and so powerful a medicine of salvation, almsgiving, by which all sins were blotted out, and yet you neglected so great a benefit. So I reproach inhumanity as the root of evil and of all impiety, and I praise love for humankind as the root of all good things. To the first I threaten eternal fire; to the second I promise the kingdom of heaven.” Your promises are beautiful, Master; beautiful too is your kingdom that we await, and also the hell that is threatened. The one urges [?] of the poor will not perish forever; in Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. ON REPENTANCE.

1. Though I was absent from you yesterday, it was not by choice but by necessity. I was absent in body, not in intention; absent in the flesh, not in the disposition of my mind. For I embraced all of you as far as I could, and carried you in my mind. Now again, brothers, having shaken off this passing illness, I have been all the more eager to see your faces. I ran to you whom I love while still bearing the remnants of the illness. The sick look for baths and bathhouses [after their illness]; but I thought it worthwhile to behold your longed-for faces and to satisfy the desire I owed to hear you, this great ocean without brine, this sea free from waves. I came to see your cleansed field. For who is such [?] [Savile: “the faces”] [?] a dove. A wolf goes in and comes out a

sheep; a snake goes in and comes out a lamb. It is not that nature is changed, but that wickedness is driven out. That is why I keep raising the subject of repentance. For repentance is dreadful and fearsome to the sinner; it is a medicine for offenses, the consuming of transgressions, the spending of tears, boldness before God, a weapon against the devil, a sword that cuts off his head, the hope of salvation, the destruction of despair. It opens heaven, it leads into paradise, it overcomes the devil (that is precisely why I keep raising this subject), just as confidence [?] causes him to be tripped up. Are you a sinner? Do not despair. I do not stop applying these medicines again and again, for I know how great a weapon against the devil it is that you do not despair. If you have sins, do not despair; I do not stop saying this again and again. Even if you sin every day, repent every day. We know what to do with old houses: when they rot, we take out the rotten parts and put in new ones, and we never forget to care for them continually. Let us do the same in ourselves. If you have grown old today through sin, renew yourself through repentance. “But is it possible,” someone asks, “for one who repents to be saved?” Entirely possible. “I have spent my whole life in sins; if I repent, will I be saved?” Certainly. “How is that clear?” From the love for humankind of your Master. Am I relying on your repentance? Is your repentance strong enough to scour away such great evils? If there were only repentance, you would be right to be afraid. But since God's love for humankind is mixed with repentance, take courage. For God's love for humankind has no measure, and his goodness cannot be expressed in words. Your wickedness has a measure, but the medicine has none. Your wickedness, whatever it may be, is human wickedness, but God's love for humankind is beyond words. So take courage, because it overcomes your wickedness. Picture a spark falling into the ocean: can it stay alight, or even be seen? What a spark is to the ocean, wickedness is to God's love for humankind. Or rather, the difference is not even that small, but far greater. For the ocean, however great, has a measure, but God's love for humankind is unbounded. I say this not to make you more careless but to make you more zealous. I have often urged you not to go up to the theater. You heard me and were not persuaded; you went up to the theater; you ignored my word. Do not be ashamed to come in again and listen. “I heard and did not keep it; how can I come in again?” For now you know this very thing, that you did not keep it. For now you are ashamed, for now you blush. For now, though no one is reproving you, you carry the bridle about with you. For now you have my word rooted in you. For now, though it does not show, my teaching is cleansing you. You did not keep it; have you condemned yourself? Then you have kept it halfway. Even if you do not keep it, but say, “I did not keep it,” the one who condemns himself for not keeping it is eager to keep it. Did you watch the show? Did you commit a transgression? Were you taken captive by the prostitute? Did you come down from the theater? So, knowing that he [God] forgives and does not allow even a trace to remain, but [?] Satan, since sin carries shame — [?] grants health and beauty, with the release [?] — a thing well able to drive the sinner away, while repentance carries boldness, a thing able to draw the penitent, reversed the order: he gave shame to repentance and boldness to sin. How so? I will tell you. Someone is seized by a fierce desire for a common prostitute. He follows the prostitute like a captive. He goes into the brothel without shame; without blushing he embraces the prostitute; he commits the sin, and nowhere is there any shame in him, nowhere does he blush. He comes out of there when the sin is over, and he is ashamed to repent. Wretch! When you were embracing the prostitute you were not ashamed, but when you came to repent, then you are ashamed? He is ashamed — tell me, why was he not ashamed when he committed fornication? He does the deed and is not ashamed, and you blush at the word? This is the devil's trickery. In sin he does not let a man feel shame, but lets him make a public show of it, for he knows that if the man feels shame he will flee from sin. In repentance he makes him feel shame, for he knows that while he is ashamed he will not repent. He does two evils: he drags him into sin, and he holds back his repentance. Why then are you ashamed? When you were committing fornication you were not ashamed; when you apply the remedy, are you ashamed? When you free yourself from sin, are you ashamed? You ought to have been ashamed then, you should have been ashamed then, when you were sinning. When you were becoming a sinner you were not ashamed; when you are becoming righteous, are you ashamed? "Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified." O the Master's love for mankind! He did not say, "so that you may not be punished," but "so that you may be justified." Was it not enough for him that you do not punish him — do you also make him righteous? Most certainly. But pay careful attention to the words: "I make him righteous." And where did he do this? In the case of the thief, when all he said to his companion was this: "Do you not even fear God? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve." The Savior says to him, "Today you will be with me in paradise." He did not say, "I release you from punishment and penalty"; rather, he brings him into paradise as a righteous man. Do you see him made righteous by confession? God's love for mankind is great: he did not spare his Son, so that he might spare the slave; he handed over the Only-begotten, so that he might buy ungrateful slaves; he paid the blood of his Son as the price. O the Master's love for mankind! And do not say to me again, "I have sinned much, and how will I be able to be saved?" If you cannot, your Master can — and in such a way as to wipe out the sins. Pay careful attention to the words: he wipes out sins in such a way that not even a trace of them remains. With bodies this is not possible. Even if the physician takes pains ten thousand times, even if he applies medicines to the wound, he does make the wound disappear; but often someone is struck in the face, and the wound is healed but the scar remains, carrying about the disfigurement of the face as proof of the wound. And the physician strives in countless ways to wipe out the scar as well, but he cannot, for the weakness of nature resists him, and

So Isaiah says, "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth": for Moses commanded that you be called today. He calls the elements not only for this reason, but also because they had dealt with the Jews. "Hear, O heaven," for you brought down the manna; "give ear, O earth," for you gave the quail. Hear, O heaven, hear, for you brought down the manna; for you, beyond nature, made a display [?]: you were above, and imitated a threshing floor. Give ear, [O earth,] for you were below, and prepared a table set out on the spot. Nature was idle, and grace was at work. There was no labor of oxen, yet the ear of grain was ready; no hands of cooks, no command [?], but the manna became everything, a sanctified spring [?]; nature forgot its own weakness. How did their clothes not wear out? How did their sandals not grow old? All things came to be for their service. "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth." After those reminders and those benefits, the Master is insulted. Whom shall I petition? Or you? I have no man who listens. "Behold, I came, and there was no man; I spoke, and there was none to hear." I speak to irrational things, since the rational have sunk to the worthlessness of irrational things. That is why another prophet too, seeing the king raving, the idol being worshipped, God being insulted, and all the others cowering, says, "Hear, O altar, hear me." Are you speaking to a stone? Yes, since the king is more insensible than a stone. "Hear me, O altar, hear: thus says the Lord." And at once the altar split apart; the stone heard, the stone burst and poured out the sacrifice. How did the man not hear? He stretched out his hand to seize the prophet; and what does God do? He withered his hand. See what he did; see the Master's love for mankind and the slave's sin. Why did he not wither his hand from the beginning? So that he might come to his senses through what happened to the stone. "For if the stone had not split, I would have spared you; but since the stone split and you were not corrected, I bring my wrath upon you." He stretched out his hand to seize the prophet, and his hand withered. The trophy stood [?] … remains insensible [?]; here [?] he says that so many bodyguards and generals and so much help were there, and they could not draw back his hand; but the hand stood giving voice, publicly proclaiming the defeat of impiety — a trophy over impiety, God's love for mankind and that man's madness. And they could not draw it back. But lest, weaving one word out of another, we forget our subject, come, let us show what we promised. What did I promise? That if someone has countless wounds, but repents and does what is good, God wipes them out in such a way that not even a scar, not a trace, not a sign of the former sins appears. for since they imitated their way of life, he also gives them their name: "Come, hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom and Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of whole burnt offerings of rams, and I do not want the fat of lambs. If you bring me fine flour, it is futile; incense is an abomination to me; my soul hates your new moons and your sabbaths; I cannot bear your fast and great day. When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you." What is equal to this wrath? The prophet calls on heaven, laments, wails, mourns, and says: It is no mere wound, no mere bruise: God is angry; he does not accept sacrifice, nor new moon, nor sabbath, nor fine flour, nor prayer, nor outstretched hands. Do you see the sore? Do you see the incurable disease — not of one, not of two, not of ten, but of thousands? What then after this? "Wash yourselves, become clean." Is there any sin that admits [?] despair? God himself says, "I do not hear you," and you say, "Wash yourselves"? Why do you say those things? Why these? Both are useful: those, so that I may frighten; these, so that I may draw them in. If you do not hear them, they have no hope of salvation; if they have no hope of salvation, how can you say, "Wash yourselves"? But he is an affectionate father, alone good, and more compassionate than a father. And so that you may learn that he is a father, he says to them, "What shall I do to you, Judah?" Do you not know what you will do? "I know, but I do not want to." The nature of the sins demands it, and the greatness of his love for mankind holds him back. "What shall I do to you?" Shall I spare you? But you will become more careless. Shall I come against you? But my love for mankind does not allow it. "What shall I do to you? Shall I make you like Sodom, and overthrow you like Gomorrah? My heart is turned." The one who is beyond passion imitates a man moved by passion — or rather an affectionate mother. "My heart is turned": what a woman would say over her child. "My heart is turned."

What are you doing, man? Did you not promise the priest, when he said, "Let us lift up our minds and hearts," and you said, "We have them to the Lord"? Are you not afraid, do you not blush to be found a liar at that very fearful hour? Oh, the wonder of it! The mystical table is prepared, the Lamb of God is slain for you, the priest struggles for you, spiritual fire wells up from the spotless table, the Cherubim stand by and the Seraphim fly, the six-winged ones cover their faces, all the bodiless powers intercede for you together with the priest, the spiritual fire descends, the blood is poured into the chalice from the spotless side for your cleansing — and are you not afraid, do you not blush to be found a liar at this fearful hour? The week has one hundred and sixty-eight hours; God has set apart one single hour for himself; and you spend even this on worldly affairs, on jokes and chatter? With what boldness, then, do you approach the mysteries? With what defiled conscience? If you were carrying dung in your hands, would you dare to touch the hem of the earthly king's robe?
